notes.text:
And set me down — So it seemed to me in the vision. Which is a lively representation of a threefold resurrection:

1. Of the resurrection of souls, from the death of sin, to the life of righteousness:

2. The resurrection of the church from an afflicted state, to liberty and peace:

3. The resurrection of the body at the great day, especially the bodies of believers to life eternal.
And he — The Lord.

Prophesied — Declared these promises. As I prophesied - While I was prophesying. A noise - A rattling of the bones in their motion. A shaking - A trembling or commotion among the bones, enough to manifest a divine presence, working among them. Came together - Glided nearer and nearer, 'till each bone met the bone to which it was to be joined. Of all the bones of all those numerous slain, not one was missing, not one missed its way, not one missed its place, but each knew and found its fellow. Thus in the resurrection of the dead, the scattered atoms shall be arranged in their proper place and order, and every bone come to his bone, by the same wisdom and power by which they were first formed in the womb of her that is with child.
Came up — Gradually spreading itself.
Prophesy — Declare what my will is. O breath - The soul, whose emblem here is wind; which, as it gently blew upon these lifeless creatures, each was inspired with its own soul or spirit.
And the breath — The spirit of life, or the soul, Gen. ii, 7.
The whole house — The emblem of the house of Israel. Are dried - Our state is as hopeless, as far from recovery, as dried bones are from life.
I will open — Though your captivity be as death, your persons close as the grave, yet I will open those graves.
Mark — Observe them accurately and punish them as they deserve. Stand - At thy tribunal.

Forgiveness — Thou art able and ready to forgive repenting sinners. Feared - Not with a slavish, but with a childlike fear. This mercy of thine is the foundation of all religion, without which men would desperately proceed in their impious courses.
I wait — That he would pardon my sins.
They — Whether soldiers that keep the night-watches in an army, or the priests or Levites who did so in the temple.

Israel — Every true Israelite. Plenteous - Abundantly sufficient for all persons who accept it upon God's terms. David testifies his humility, and exhorts Israel to trust in God, ver. 1-3. A song of degrees of David.

glossa.text:
*A canticle of degrees.* ((ID.)) The eleventh degree, etc., *as far as* a glad conclusion is set down with the certainty of pardon, there, *Let Israel hope in the Lord.*

*Out of the depths.* ((AUG.)) He who feels himself in the deep, etc., *as far as* as the Scripture says: *The sinner, when he shall have come into the depth of vices, contemneth.*

*Who shall abide it.* ((ID.)) Because well nigh all human life is barked at round about by sins, and every conscience is accused by its own thoughts. That heart is not chaste which presumes upon its own justice. Let it therefore presume upon the mercy of God, *For with him there is propitiation,* whence he subjoins:

*For with thee there is propitiation.* As it were: In what hope dost thou cry? Because there is mercy in thee, wherefore he speaks thus: Or join it thus.

((AUG.)) No man can abide it, etc., *as far as* one hope therefore there is: *For with thee there is propitiation,* etc., *For thy law's sake,* ((ID.)) I have waited for the *law* of mercy, etc., *as far as* and thou hast given this law in the very necessity.

*The morning.* ((ID.)) Let him hope in the morning watch who hopes for nothing else from God than immortality. *From the morning watch,* etc., *as far as* thence in the law the head and the tail of the victim were offered to the Lord. *Let Israel hope in the Lord.* ((CASS.)) The second part, where is the glad conclusion: Secure concerning himself, he preaches that they should hope always in the Lord. As it were, as his soul has hoped, so let Israel hope.
*And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities.* ((ID.)) Here he has now said what that one shall do, whom he called merciful and plentiful.

notes.text: For to be carnally minded — That is, to mind the things of the flesh. Is death - The sure mark of spiritual death, and the way to death everlasting. But to be spiritually minded - That is, to mind the things of the Spirit. Is life - A sure mark of spiritual life, and the way to life everlasting. And attended with peace - The peace of God, which is the foretaste of life everlasting; and peace with God, opposite to the enmity mentioned in the next verse.
Enmity against God — His existence, power, and providence.
They who are in the flesh — Under the government of it.

In the Spirit — Under his government. If any man have not the Spirit of Christ - Dwelling and governing in him. He is none of his - He is not a member of Christ; not a Christian; not in a state of salvation. A plain, express declaration, which admits of no exception. He that hath ears to hear, let him hear!

Now if Christ be in you — Where the Spirit of Christ is, there is Christ. The body indeed is dead - Devoted to death. Because of sin - Heretofore committed. But the Spirit is life - Already truly alive. Because of righteousness - Now attained. From ver. 13, St. Paul, having finished what he had begun, chap. vi, 1, describes purely the state of believers.

glossa.text: *For the prudence.* He who savours these things which are of the flesh is not just; for the prudence of the flesh is death. *Life and peace.* Life indeed referred to this, *the affection of the flesh is death;* but peace to that which follows: *the affection of the flesh is enmity toward God.*

*Because the wisdom of the flesh.* By enumerating these things he deters from obedience to the flesh.

*It is an enemy.* While it thinks God can do nothing beyond what is seen in the natures of things.

*If yet.* He speaks ambiguously, because they are not yet of perfect faith, but there is hope of their being perfected. *The Spirit of God.* The Spirit of Christ, because the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are the same.

*The body indeed.* By the name of the body he signifies the whole man, as Ezekiel conversely by the name of the soul, when he says: *The soul that hath sinned,* etc. And the sense is: If the spirit of Christ is in you, although the body be dead, that is, although the man be dead because of sins, that is, in sins, yet the spirit, that is, the soul which had been ungodly, lives: because it is joined to God, who is life, and this because of justification, that is, the remission of sins, which is from the Holy Spirit. *Dead,* he says, not mortal. For before sin the body was animal, that is, mortal, namely able to die. But which it was not necessary to die: now it is called dead because of sin, that is, because it is necessary to die. *Because of sin* to be shunned, this weakness is kept back, that thereby he may the more fear to sin.

*But if the Spirit. ((AUG.))* Mark that the Holy Spirit, etc., *as far as* even as who shall declare the generation of the Son?

*He shall quicken also your mortal. ((ID.))* Behold the fourth act. In the first action, etc., *as far as* because we had forsaken God who is above us.

*Mortal.* Not dead, because in the resurrection, when this mortal shall put on immortality, not only the necessity of dying, which it now has because of sin, but not even the mortality which the animal body had before sin, shall remain.

*Because of him that dwelleth.* It appears most evidently that man deserved, because of sin, the death not only of the spirit but also of the body, and that through the Holy Spirit both were delivered by Christ.

notes.text: One Lazarus — It is probable, Lazarus was younger than his sisters. Bethany is named, the town of Mary and Martha, and Lazarus is mentioned after them, ver. 5. Ecclesiastical history informs us, that Lazarus was now thirty years old, and that he lived thirty years after Christ's ascension.
It was that Mary who afterward anointed, &c. She was more known than her elder sister Martha, and as such is named before her.

This sickness is not to death, but for the glory of God — The event of this sickness will not be death, in the usual sense of the word, a final separation of his soul and body; but a manifestation of the glorious power of God.
Let us go into Judea — From the country east of Jordan, whither he had retired some time before, when the Jews sought to stone him, chap. x, 39, 40.

Are there not twelve hours in the day? — The Jews always divided the space from sunrise to sunset, were the days longer or shorter, into twelve parts: so that the hours of their day were all the year the same in number, though much shorter in winter than in summer. If any man walk in the day he stumbleth not - As if he had said, So there is such a space, a determined time, which God has allotted me. During that time I stumble not, amidst all the snares that are laid for me. Because he seeth the light of this world - And so I see the light of God surrounding me.
But if a man walk in the night — If he have not light from God; if his providence does no longer protect him.

Our friend Lazarus sleepeth — This he spoke, just when he died. Sleepeth - Such is the death of good men in the language of heaven. But the disciples did not yet understand this language. And the slowness of our understanding makes the Scripture often descend to our barbarous manner of speaking.
Thomas in Hebrew, as Didymus in Greek, signifies a twin. With him — With Jesus, whom he supposed the Jews would kill. It seems to be the language of despair.
Mary sat in the house — Probably not hearing what was said.
Whatsoever thou wilt ask, God will give it thee — So that she already believed he could raise him from the dead.
l am the resurrection — Of the dead. And the life - Of the living. He that believeth in me, though he die, yet shall he live - In life everlasting.
She fell at his feet — This Martha had not done. So she makes amends for her slowness in coming.

He groaned — So he restrained his tears. So he stopped them soon after, ver. 38. He troubled himself - An expression amazingly elegant, and full of the highest propriety. For the affections of Jesus were not properly passions, but voluntary emotions, which were wholly in his own power. And this tender trouble which he now voluntarily sustained, was full of the highest order and reason.
Jesus wept — Out of sympathy with those who were in tears all around him, as well as from a deep sense of the misery sin had brought upon human nature.
Could not this person have even caused, that this man should not have died? — Yet they never dreamed that he could raise him again! What a strange mixture of faith and unbelief.

It was a cave — So Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and their wives, except Rachel, were buried in the cave of Machpelah, Gen. xlix, 29-31. These caves were commonly in rocks, which abounded in that country, either hollowed by nature or hewn by art. And the entrance was shut up with a great stone, which sometimes had a monumental inscription.
Lord, by this time he stinketh — Thus did reason and faith struggle together.
Said I not — It appears by this, that Christ had said more to Martha than is before recorded.

Jesus lifted up his eyes — Not as if he applied to his Father for assistance. There is not the least show of this. He wrought the miracle with an air of absolute sovereignty, as the Lord of life and death. But it was as if he had said, I thank thee, that by the disposal of thy providence, thou hast granted my desire, in this remarkable opportunity of exerting my power, and showing forth thy praise.
He cried with a loud voice — That all who were present might hear. Lazarus, come forth - Jesus called him out of the tomb as easily as if he had been not only alive, but awake also.

And he came forth bound hand and foot with grave clothes — Which were wrapt round each hand and each foot, and his face was wrapt about with a napkin - If the Jews buried as the Egyptians did, the face was not covered with it, but it only went round the forehead, and under the chin; so that he might easily see his way.
Many believed on Him — And so the Son of God was glorified, according to what our Lord had said, ver. 4.

glossa.text: *Now there was.* While he tarries beyond the Jordan, Lazarus falls sick, and the sisters send to him there. These sisters of Lazarus are a figure of the Jews already received into eternal blessedness, who for the healing of their brother, that is, for the rest still wandering in the darkness of ignorance, beseech the Lord out of their most familiar manner of acting. *Lazarus was sick.* Lazarus is a figure of the Jews who were weak in the faith of Christ: Martha and Mary signify the teaching of the good Jews.

*Behold, he whom thou lovest,* etc. Lazarus, by whom the sinner is signified, who is loved by the Lord, because he came not to call the just but sinners. The sisters are the sinner's good thoughts, which pray for the loosing of his sins.
*For the glory of God,* etc. That is, that the Son of God may be glorified. Behold, he calls himself God, against those who say that the Son of God is not God.
*He loved.* The Saviour of the sick and the raiser of the dead loved Lazarus, because he was sick and dead.

*Two days.* That the four days might be fulfilled. For on the first day, on which it was announced to him, the sick man died beyond the Jordan; for two days he remained: behold, three; but on the fourth day he came.
*Let us go into Judea.* Mystically: it signifies that faith is to return to the Jews at the end through Elias and Enoch.

*The disciples say to him.* Terrified, wishing to give counsel to their master that he should not die, as elsewhere Peter also: *Far be it from thee, Lord,* this shall not be unto thee. But as Peter is praised for what is another's: *Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-Jona, because the Father hath revealed it to thee,* he is blamed for what is his own: *Go back behind me, Satan, because thou savourest not the things that are of God, but the things that are of man.* So too he rebuked these, saying that he is the day in which they ought to walk lest they stumble, and that walking without him they stumble, as now unwilling that he should die who came to die for men. But he says that they are the hours which follow the day, not days, but the day enlightens them. Twelve is a consecrated number which remains complete: for when Judas was cast down, who did not shine among the hours, another is substituted.
*Are there not twelve hours. ((HIER.))* Christ is the day, and in another manner the apostles are the day, as Christ is, etc., *as far as* they are understood to be the twelve apostles.
*That you may believe.* Not that they should only now begin to believe, but that they might believe more robustly. For their faith was always increased by miracles.
*And he found. ((AUG.))* Mystically: there are four days of death. A man is born, etc., *as far as* but mercy does not leave behind even such as these.

*But now also I know.* This I know, that thou canst raise him if thou wilt; which I leave to thy judgment. But I do not presume, nor do I ask that thou raise him, since I know not whether the resurrection be useful to be done.

*Yea, though he be dead.* Jesus raised three dead men: one in the house, that is, in the heart; a second at the gate, that is, in the mouth; a third in the tomb, that is, in the deed and the habit of sinning. *He shall live.* As Abraham, Isaac and Jacob live, whose God he is called as of the living. The believer, though dead, lives, as the unbeliever, though living, is dead.

*Secretly.* Because if the Jews had heard that she had been called by Jesus, she would not follow, and so they would not see the miracle. But because they thought that they were going to their brother's tomb, they followed. *And calleth thee.* By reason of brevity in Martha's words he shows what was not said before, that is, that the Lord had called Mary.
*They followed.* The evangelist took care to relate this, that we might see what occasion brought it about that the resurrection of the man four days dead should have more witnesses.

*He groaned in the spirit.* Note the power: he himself groaned and troubled himself, whom another could not trouble, as he took upon himself all things of this kind because he willed it. And it signifies how greatly a man ought to be troubled when pressed by so great a mass of sin. But when the sinner, reckoning what good things of God he has received and what evils he has rendered, groans in spirit and is troubled, Christ groans in him and is troubled, because faith concerning Christ is Christ in the heart. But faith groans in a man while he rebukes himself for his sins.

*Where have you laid him?* He who though absent knew that he was dead knows also where he is buried; but speaking thus, he signifies that he as it were does not know the lost man; whence it is said: *I know you not ((Matth. VII))*. And: *Where is Adam? ((Gen. III.))*

*Jesus therefore,* etc. He shows the difficulty of the quickening of such a sinner. *Now it was a cave.* Morally: every sinner pressed by the mass of his sins and weighed down by his own law, and now stinking by his own evil habit, openly corrupts others by his bad example: the sisters are certain thoughts, because sometimes, thinking that he has done ill, he grieves.
*Lord, by this time he stinketh.* She feared that, the stone being taken away, the stench would rather be stirred up than her brother raised.

*But for the people,* etc. By these words he shows that he seeks the glory of the Father, as in his other works. For because according to his manhood he was less than the Father, he asks of him the raising of Lazarus, and therefore says that he was heard, and this for the sake of the bystanders, that they might so believe him the Son of God.

*With a loud voice.* He groaned, he wept, he cried out, because he rises with difficulty whom the mass of an evil habit presses; but nevertheless after the great voice he rises, that is, by the great grace of God he is quickened while he repents.

*And forthwith he came forth.* While the sinner despises, he lies buried; when he repents, he rises; when he confesses, he comes forth, as though going out of hiding into the open. *Loose him.* Christ by himself quickens within; to his ministers he grants the power of loosing.

O God, just as we look into a mirror to see any soiled spots on our face
Out of the depths I cry to thee

registers.label: Spare
lines: Out of the depths we cry to you, O Lord.
With you there is forgiveness; our souls wait for you.
Can these bones live? Only you know, O God.
Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe.
Lazarus, come out; unbind him, and let him go.
You are the resurrection and the life.
Roll back the stone; come, let us worship.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: A valley floor white with bones, dry as chalk, picked clean by years; and a voice asking, mortal, can these live?
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Then a rattling, bone to its bone, sinew and skin, and the wind comes from the four corners and they stand and breathe.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Out of our own depths we wait for you more than the watchman waits for the morning; with you there is forgiveness.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
At a sealed grave you wept, and then you called a dead man by name, and he came out still wrapped in the cloths.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
You are the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in you will live. Come, let us worship.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Breathe on us. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Out of the depths we wait for you, O Lord.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Come from the four winds, O breath, and let these bones live.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
You call us by name from the grave: come out.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
You are resurrection and life. Come, let us worship.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.
